description:
We are multimedia engineers from Barranquilla, and we want to create a website that showcases the history of NASA’s discarded equipment in an interactive and engaging way. 

We have skills in storytelling, UX/UI design, and programming; if you’re interested in 3D modeling and are good at it, you’re more than welcome to join us! :)
summary:
The Lost Space Archive is an interactive, story-driven educational web experience designed for children ages 8-10. Created in response to NASA's “Abandoned but not Forgotten” challenge, it brings the stories of six exploration vehicles and robotic explorers left on the Moon and Mars to life.

Through an illustrated space archive, young explorers can discover missions, explore interactive planetary maps, meet the machines through character-based storytelling, and complete learning activities to recover fragments of their scientific legacy. The experience combines NASA mission information with playful narratives, visual exploration, and interactive challenges to make space science more accessible and engaging.

Available in English and Spanish, the project aims to spark curiosity about planetary exploration and help young learners understand that even machines left behind can leave a lasting scientific legacy.
details:
The Lost Space Archive is a bilingual, interactive educational web experience inspired by NASA's “Abandoned but not Forgotten” challenge. It introduces children ages 8–10 to the robotic explorers and scientific equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars, helping them understand the missions, discoveries, and scientific contributions of these machines.

The experience is organized around a fictional Memory Station, guided by Spark, a friendly robot who invites young explorers to recover forgotten mission records. From the station, users can choose between Mars and the Moon, explore illustrated mission maps, select historical explorers, and open interactive mission dossiers. The project features six real exploration vehicles and robotic explorers: Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Ingenuity, Surveyor 3, and the Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle.

Each dossier presents historical context, mission objectives, discoveries, instruments, and relevant milestones, with references to NASA sources. Users can also complete simplified educational challenges related to the missions, collect memory fragments, and unlock a constellation of discoveries as they progress.

The application combines factual scientific information with fictional character personalities and storytelling. This approach makes complex space exploration topics more approachable without presenting fictional dialogue as historical fact. The experience is available in English and Spanish, includes interactive visual elements and optional spoken narration, and stores progress locally in the browser without requiring an account. It also features a responsive design that adapts to different screen sizes, providing a consistent and user-friendly experience across smartphones, tablets, laptops, and desktop computers.

The project was developed using React, TypeScript, Vite, CSS, and SVG illustrations. Local structured data files organize mission information and its references, while browser storage preserves the user's progress.

Our goal is to encourage curiosity, support early STEM learning, and show young audiences that even equipment left behind on distant worlds can continue to contribute to humanity's understanding of space.
